chunks: "A motor draws the most current when it's not turning: at startup or when it's stalled.
A spinning motor generates a back-EMF proportional to speed, and that subtracts from the supply. So the current is V minus K e omega over R.
At omega equals zero there's no back-EMF, so the current is V over R, limited only by the coil resistance.
With a 12 volts supply and a 1 ohm winding, that's 12 amps, versus half an amp when it's spinning freely.
The same applies when the shaft is jammed or heavily loaded, since a higher load means a lower speed and more current to make the torque.

Strictly, the inductance delays the current for a few milliseconds, with a time constant L over R, so the peak is a bit below V over R and happens a few milliseconds after turn-on, before the speed picks up.
A solenoid is simpler: it's an inductor with resistance, and in DC its current rises to V over R and stays there, so the most current is at steady state, after the plunger has closed.
During the stroke the inductance changes, which makes the current dip, but then it rises to V over R.
AC solenoids are different: with the plunger open the inductance is low, so inrush current can be several times the holding current."
